speaker_role: test-prep/consultancy marketer (Rob Franek, editor-in-chief of The Princeton Review)
commercial_incentive: yes; The Princeton Review is a for-profit test-prep company, and the video promotes princetonreview.com as a data source
key_insights: Test-optional means a student isn't penalized for withholding scores, but a school may still weigh submitted scores, so two otherwise-similar applicants aren't on equal footing if only one submits
Recommends comparing a student's SAT/ACT score to a school's published 50% mean: submit if well above it, withhold if well below
Notes students apply to an average of 7-9 schools, and if even one requires scores, that alone can necessitate testing regardless of other schools' test-optional status
Scores remain tied to scholarship opportunities and honors-college/program admission at many schools even when general admission is test-optional
Because mostly higher-scoring students have been the ones submitting under test-optional policies, average reported SAT/ACT scores at many colleges have risen
specific_numbers_or_facts: About 1,000 colleges were already test-optional pre-pandemic (2019); nearly 3,000 became test-optional overnight during the pandemic (Rob Franek)
The Princeton Review surveys nearly 2,500 four-year colleges for score data (Rob Franek)
Students apply to an average of 7-9 colleges (Rob Franek)
notable_or_distinctive: gives a clear, specific decision rule (submit if above the published 50% mean, withhold if below) rather than vague 'it depends' guidance
reliability_notes: presenter's firm sells test prep, an inherent incentive to encourage testing, though the core decision-rule advice is standard counseling guidance; figures are presented as the firm's own survey data without independent verification
